A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GravMAD and retain matching formulations, experiments, and results. The complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, equations, and algorithms, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original RLBench experiments on 12 base and 8 novel tasks, component ablations, and failure-case analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, scalability experiments, additional novel-task tests, and evaluations on 10 physical-robot tasks.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 adds an occupancy-derived avoidance map, smoothing and combining it with the distance cost. It also explicitly separates training-time random offsets from inference. These refine the reported map-generation procedure; the sub-goal discovery rules, diffusion architecture, and losses remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained 12 base and 8 novel simulation tasks, v4 evaluates Push Buttons Shape, Button Close Jar, and Pour From Cup to Cup, plus six base and four novel physical-robot tasks (Appendices D.4 and D.6). This substantially extends coverage to physical environments, skill composition, and unfamiliar objects and interactions.

E2.justification: The original VoxPoser, Act3D, and 3D Diffuser Actor comparisons remain. Table 7 adds VoxPoser (Manual), supplied with ground-truth object poses, and ChainedDiffuser (Oracle), supplied with ideal keyposes. Table 8 adds only ChainedDiffuser (Oracle). These are targeted extensions to the existing comparator suite.

E3.justification: v4 adds demonstration-count and camera-view sweeps, thresholded position/rotation accuracy metrics, runtime measurements, and a physical-robot protocol using 20 demonstrations per base task and 10 evaluation episodes per task. The original RLBench training and testing budgets remain. Table 5 and Appendix B.2.7 also revise the conditional block color from blue to black, without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 substantially extends the original ablations and failure analysis with data/viewpoint sensitivity, runtime comparisons, keypose-filtering and touch-force case studies, and harder generalization probes. Appendix D.5 adds a no-cost-map ablation with gripper closure encoded as -1, addressing the encoder failure that confounded the original zero-success ablation.

E5.justification: The original three-seed evaluation and numerical uncertainty entries in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. New Figure 14 contains shaded bands, but its caption and Appendix D.3 do not define their meaning or associated run counts. Whether these introduce statistical uncertainty reporting, rather than another plotting convention, cannot be reliably determined.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and Figure 4 retain their results. Added findings include 62.66% success on Push Buttons Shape and zero on the other two added simulation tasks (Table 10), 10–100% across physical tasks (Table 11), and 44.75%/41.88% base/novel success for the differently encoded no-cost-map ablation (Figure 16). Baseline, runtime, and scaling results are also added. Table 8 reports a ChainedDiffuser average of 43.22%, although its displayed task scores average 50.04%, an unexplained discrepancy.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 revises the mathematical cost-map construction from normalized Euclidean distance to a renormalized combination of twice that distance cost plus a smoothed occupancy map. This is a limited definition change. The problem assumptions and diffusion/loss equations (1)–(6) remain unchanged, with no added theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion add explicit claims of real-world task reasoning and generalization; v1 leaves physical-robot validation to future work. The central hybrid-method contributions and headline simulation improvement claims remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendices C–E add substantive explanations of training–inference distribution shifts, omitted rotation guidance, heuristic limitations, latency, skill-composition failures, and possible alternatives to GravMap representations. The cost-map ablation explanation changes from non-unit quaternion predictions to an encoder/zero-gradient problem. These materially expand and qualify the earlier interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v4 documents the physical-robot setup, RealSense D435i camera, image resizing, MoveIt/BiRRT execution, and demonstration/evaluation procedures. It also specifies the added oracle baselines and avoidance-map parameters, including the target exclusion radius and Gaussian smoothing. These substantially extend implementation coverage, while Table 3 and the existing prompt/video access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v4 explicitly acknowledges earlier sub-goal approaches, adding references including Black, Kang, and Ma, and cites Garcia for task categorization. Appendix C.1 further distinguishes GravMap processing from VoxPoser. Additional references support proposed future extensions, while the broader imitation-learning/foundation-model positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include local wording and terminology corrections, publication-header and acknowledgment additions, moving Algorithm 1 into Appendix A, and organizing the expanded supplementary discussion, results, and limitations into Appendices C–E.

P2.justification: v4 substantially expands the visual presentation with task taxonomies, keypose and force illustrations, scaling curves, additional-task examples, a revised ablation display, physical-robot visuals, and Tables 6–11. Earlier figures are largely retained and relocated or renumbered; the original two main result tables are separated across pages.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the simulation-only evidence in v1 through physical-robot validation, targeted comparator controls, and scalability and generalization tests. The revised cost-map ablation addresses an important experimental confound, while explicit failures and expanded limitations better establish applicability boundaries. Physical tests remain small and lack baseline comparisons, and Table 8 has an unexplained aggregate discrepancy, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and interpretation.
